```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("../setup.R")
docs_setup(legend = "right")
has_png <- requireNamespace("png", quietly = TRUE)
has_lidr <- requireNamespace("lidR", quietly = TRUE)
```

A 3D scan arrives as a file: a textured mesh from a phone or tablet LiDAR app, a coloured point cloud from photogrammetry, or a LAS file from an airborne survey. This article reads each kind, draws it, and ends with a surface rebuilt from scanned points. Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html); the textured mesh needs [png](https://cran.r-project.org/package=png) (JPEG textures need [jpeg](https://cran.r-project.org/package=jpeg)), and the airborne example uses the sample data of [lidR](https://cran.r-project.org/package=lidR).

1. Read a textured mesh with `read_mesh_3d()`.

2. Read a point cloud with `read_points_3d()`.

3. Rebuild a surface from the points with `stat_implicit_fit_3d()`.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
```

## Textured meshes

Scanning apps on phones and tablets with a LiDAR sensor (Polycam, Scaniverse, 3d Scanner App on iPhone and iPad Pro models) export a mesh as OBJ, PLY or glTF (`.glb`), with the camera images baked into one texture. The example below writes such an export: a scanned stone as an OBJ file whose `vt` lines give texture coordinates, an MTL file naming the texture, and the texture as a PNG. Like most scanner exports, it puts the vertical axis on y.

<details><summary>Code that writes the scan files</summary>

```{r scan-files, eval = has_png}
dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "stone")
dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
grid <- expand.grid(u = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 49), v = seq(0, pi, length.out = 25))
r <- with(grid, 1 + 0.08 * sin(5 * u) * sin(3 * v) + 0.05 * cos(7 * v))
xyz <- with(grid, cbind(r * cos(u) * sin(v), -r * cos(v), r * sin(u) * sin(v)))
id <- function(i, j) (j - 1) * 49 + i
q <- expand.grid(i = 1:48, j = 1:24)
faces <- with(q, cbind(id(i, j), id(i + 1, j), id(i + 1, j + 1), id(i, j + 1)))
triangles <- rbind(faces[q$j > 1, c(1, 2, 3)], faces[q$j < 24, c(1, 3, 4)])
face_lines <- sprintf("f %d/%d %d/%d %d/%d",
  triangles[, 1], triangles[, 1], triangles[, 2], triangles[, 2],
  triangles[, 3], triangles[, 3])
tex <- array(0, c(64, 128, 3))
shade <- outer(seq(0.35, 0.75, length.out = 64), 0.15 * sin(seq(0, 12 * pi, length.out = 128)), "+")
tex[, , 1] <- shade; tex[, , 2] <- 0.85 * shade; tex[, , 3] <- 0.6 * shade
png::writePNG(pmin(pmax(tex, 0), 1), file.path(dir, "stone.png"))
writeLines(c("newmtl stone", "Kd 1 1 1", "map_Kd stone.png"), file.path(dir, "stone.mtl"))
writeLines(c("mtllib stone.mtl",
  sprintf("v %.5f %.5f %.5f", xyz[, 1], xyz[, 2], xyz[, 3]),
  sprintf("vt %.5f %.5f", grid$u / (2 * pi), 1 - grid$v / pi),
  "usemtl stone",
  face_lines), file.path(dir, "stone.obj"))
```

</details>

`read_mesh_3d()` returns the corner table: one row per face corner, with the positions, the texture coordinates `.texture_u` and `.texture_v`, and the material name from `usemtl`. The texture image travels with it as the attribute `"texture"`.

```{r read-scan, eval = has_png}
stone <- read_mesh_3d(file.path(dir, "stone.obj"))
head(stone[c(".face", ".corner", "x", "y", "z", ".texture_u", ".texture_v", "material")], 4)
attr(stone, "texture")
```

Given as the layer's data, the mesh drapes its own texture. `coord_3d(up = "y")` stands the stone upright, since the file's vertical axis is y.

```{r draw-scan, eval = has_png, fig.alt = "A rounded stone with a bumpy surface, textured with brown horizontal bands from the scan image."}
ggplot() +
  geom_mesh_3d(data = stone, shading = "smooth") +
  coord_3d(up = "y")
```

A glTF or GLB export reads the same way, its node transforms applied and its embedded image taken as the texture. A file with several texture images gets them packed into one atlas.

## Point clouds

A point cloud has no faces: each row is one measured point, often with a colour from the camera and a normal estimated by the scanner. `read_points_3d()` reads PLY, LAS, XYZ, PTS and glTF point clouds into a data frame. The example writes a binary PLY of 4000 coloured points on the same stone, with a little noise along the normal, as a scan of its surface would have.

```{r point-file}
set.seed(4)
n <- 4000
u <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi); v <- acos(runif(n, -1, 1))
r <- 1 + 0.08 * sin(5 * u) * sin(3 * v) + 0.05 * cos(7 * v) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.01)
cloud <- cbind(r * cos(u) * sin(v), -r * cos(v), r * sin(u) * sin(v))
brightness <- 0.8 + 0.4 * (cloud[, 2] + 1.2) / 2.4
rgb <- round(255 * outer(brightness, c(0.55, 0.45, 0.3)))
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".ply")
con <- file(path, "wb")
writeLines(c("ply", "format binary_little_endian 1.0", paste("element vertex", n),
  "property float x", "property float y", "property float z",
  "property uchar red", "property uchar green", "property uchar blue", "end_header"), con, sep = "\n")
bytes <- rbind(matrix(writeBin(as.vector(t(cloud)), raw(), size = 4, endian = "little"), 12),
               t(matrix(as.raw(pmin(rgb, 255)), n)))
writeBin(as.vector(bytes), con)
close(con)
```

The reader keeps every vertex property of the file as a column; `red`, `green` and `blue` become one `colour` column of hex codes, which `I()` passes to the plot unscaled.

```{r read-points, fig.alt = "Four thousand brown points outlining the stone, lighter towards the top."}
points <- read_points_3d(path)
head(points, 3)
ggplot(points, aes(x, y, z = z, colour = I(colour))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4) +
  coord_3d(up = "y")
```

Files from 3D Gaussian splatting tools are PLY point clouds too; their parameters (`f_dc_0`, `opacity`, `scale_0`, `rot_0` and the rest) arrive as columns by name.

## Drawing points as splats

`geom_splat_3d()` draws each point as a Gaussian. `size` gives its standard deviation in the coordinate units of the scan. Overlapping footprints form a continuous surface.

```{r point-splats, fig.alt = "The scanned stone drawn with overlapping brown Gaussian splats."}
ggplot(points, aes(x, y, z = z, colour = I(colour))) +
  geom_splat_3d(size = 0.055) +
  coord_3d(up = "y")
```

A 3D Gaussian splatting capture stores logarithmic scales, quaternion rotations, logit opacity and spherical-harmonic colour coefficients. The layer activates these columns automatically. Here six anisotropic Gaussians carry degree-zero colour coefficients, which give the same colour from every direction.

```{r gaussian-capture, fig.alt = "Six overlapping anisotropic Gaussians in blue, green and orange."}
capture <- data.frame(x = c(-0.6, 0, 0.6, -0.6, 0, 0.6),
  y = rep(c(-0.25, 0.25), each = 3), z = c(0, 0.1, 0, 0.1, 0, 0.1),
  scale_0 = log(0.28), scale_1 = log(0.13), scale_2 = log(0.06),
  opacity = qlogis(0.9), rot_0 = 2, rot_1 = 0, rot_2 = 0, rot_3 = 0)
colours <- t(grDevices::col2rgb(rep(c("steelblue", "seagreen", "coral"), 2))) / 255
for (k in 0:2) capture[[paste0("f_dc_", k)]] <- (colours[, k + 1] - 0.5) / 0.28209479177387814
ggplot(capture, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_splat_3d() +
  xlim(-1.5, 1.5) + ylim(-0.8, 0.8) + scale_z_continuous(limits = c(-0.25, 0.35)) +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

`sh_degree` limits the spherical-harmonic degree used for a capture's view-dependent colour. The default uses every available coefficient, up to degree three. Explicit colour, fill, alpha, scale and quaternion aesthetics override the corresponding capture properties.

## Rebuilding a surface

`stat_implicit_fit_3d()` with `method = "poisson"` fits screened Poisson surface reconstruction to the points (Kazhdan and Hoppe [2013](https://doi.org/10.1145/2487228.2487237)). The file holds no normals, so the stat estimates each point's normal from its 10 nearest neighbours and orients them outwards. `depth` sets the finest octree cell, here 1.1 / 2^6 of the stone's width.

```{r rebuild, fig.alt = "A closed smooth surface rebuilt from the points, the same bumpy stone shape, in grey."}
ggplot(points, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  stat_implicit_fit_3d(method = "poisson", depth = 6, fill = "grey70", colour = NA) +
  coord_3d(up = "y")
```

## Airborne laser scanning

A LAS file stores a survey's points with their return number, classification and scan angle. `read_points_3d()` reads uncompressed LAS 1.0 to 1.4 files natively; compressed LAZ files are read by lidR (`lidR::readLAS()`, then `fortify()`). The chunk below writes a thinned sample of lidR's mixed conifer stand to an uncompressed `.las` file and reads it back.

```{r las, eval = has_lidr}
laz <- system.file("extdata", "MixedConifer.laz", package = "lidR")
las <- lidR::readLAS(laz, filter = "-keep_random_fraction 0.1")
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".las")
lidR::writeLAS(las, file)
stand <- read_points_3d(file)
nrow(stand)
table(stand$return_number)
vapply(stand[c("x", "y", "z")], function(v) diff(range(v)), numeric(1))
```

The coordinates are projected metres, and the last line gives the extent of the stand along each axis. Colouring by height shows the crowns above the ground returns.

```{r las-plot, eval = has_lidr, fig.alt = "A forest stand as points, ground returns dark at the bottom and tree crowns in lighter colours above."}
ggplot(stand, aes(x, y, z = z, colour = z)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.2) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Height (m)") +
  coord_3d(aspect = c(1, 1, 0.4))
```
